title: Predictions cross-family check
checker: OpenAI GPT-6-based Codex; exact model variant not exposed

blind_order.notes: All53answers were committed and pushed before restricted contents were shown to the reviewer. A full-index privacy scanner was started before that commit and completed later; it internally reads tracked files, including restricted ones, but returned only pass/fail. Per-file access times were not logged, so strict filesystem isolation cannot be claimed. The PartA answers remain unchanged; corrections occur only in Comparison.

method.requests: Fresh direct HTTP, sequential, manual redirects; >=8 seconds between same-host request starts. Hashes are response-body SHA-256, not extracted text.
method.found: yes means lexical passage found with PDF wrapping/line-end hyphenation and HTML/typographic spacing normalised; editorial ellipsis is not verbatim. yes does not authenticate a historical live-page version.
method.limits: No outcome assessment. No Wikipedia evidence. Survey predictor is the report. No relative horizon converted to a calendar year. Machine agreement is not human acceptance.
method.comparison_scope: All53brief items compared against verdicts and current pack. Several verdict confidence:none fields are stale relative to the already-fixed pack; no duplicate disagreement is counted for those fixes.
method.counts: 53item outcomes only. Minor includes resolved access holds and corrections to the checker’s frozen notes; model questions,15retrieval groups and16Metaculus slots are separate.
checks: Full-index privacy scan passed2052files; later scans scoped to the two changed reports
URL hygiene, maximum50words per retrieval passage, no derived dates and HTTP pacing
method.limitations: No source-outcome assessment. No human acceptance. Several exact historical publication dates remain supplied bibliographic metadata rather than independent fresh body checks. No original Mind superscript check, full Minsky/Simon1965 book passage, original Nature poll or requested Kurzweil edition/page check is claimed.

partA.event: play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 per cent chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning
partA.probability: none (70 per cent is an interrogator identification chance, not forecast confidence)
partA.confidence: I believe; it will be possible
partA.conditions_hedges: with a storage capacity of about 109; after five minutes of questioning
partA.source_date: 1950 in transcription bibliographic heading; October supplied by brief, not printed here
partA.problems: The supplied transcription visibly prints 109, without a superscript. Do not silently repair it from this copy or convert the relative horizon to a year. §6 is on PDF p.8 but the quotation is in its second paragraph.

partA.event: the use of words and general educated opinion will have altered so much that one will be able to speak of machines thinking without expecting to be contradicted
partA.horizon: at the end of the century
partA.conditions_hedges: use of words and general educated opinion
partA.source_date: 1950 in transcription heading; October not independently printed
partA.problems: A prediction about language and educated opinion, distinct from the imitation-game performance forecast.

partA.event: a significant advance can be made in one or more of these problems
partA.horizon: for a summer; during the summer of 1956
partA.conditions_hedges: if a carefully selected group of scientists work on it together for a summer
partA.source_date: August 31, 1955; proposal date on title page
partA.predictor: J. McCarthy, M. L. Minsky, N. Rochester, C. E. Shannon
partA.problems: Conditional research-progress expectation; not a claim of achieving general intelligence in 1956. Both sentences are in the single opening paragraph on PDF/printed p.2, not p.1/second paragraph. Visual check resolves broken PDF extraction.

partA.event: unknown from original (1998 reply confirms that a prediction was made and identifies its publication)
partA.conditions_hedges: unknown from original
partA.source_date: 1998-09-24; email reply; reports ORSA meeting in 1957 and publication in 1958
partA.predictor: Simon and Newell according to Simon’s retrospective reply
partA.problems: DOI redirects to INFORMS HTTP 403. Original chess wording, its page and January publication not independently verified. The email paraphrase is correct but cannot substitute for the original prediction.

partA.event: an ultraintelligent machine will be built and that it will be the last invention that man need make
partA.conditions_hedges: since it will lead to an “intelligence explosion”
partA.source_date: 1965 supplied by brief; chapter scan has no inspected publication imprint, and filename says 1966
partA.problems: §9 printed p.78/PDF p.48; line-end hyphenation normalised. Preserve both construction and last-invention wording and the author’s probability expression; filename is not publication evidence.

partA.event: computing system exhibiting intelligence at adult human level
partA.horizon: Estimated number of years before; in 20 years, in 50 years and in more than 50 years (later AI Impacts summary)
partA.conditions_hedges: sixty-seven British and American computer scientists working in, or close to, the machine intelligence field
partA.source_date: 1986 second-edition reprint; chapter headed 1973; poll “last year”; AI Impacts live retrospective summary is separately dated, not a 1972 source
partA.predictor: Michie’s survey report, separately AI Impacts’ retrospective summary
partA.problems: Fig.11.4 printed p.146/PDF p.153 visually inspected. Original report says no objective basis and plots frequencies; it does not state the AI Impacts three-way prose. Do not promote the later summary to an original estimate or make the poll Michie’s personal forecast.

partA.conditions_hedges: reported in letters to the present author
partA.source_date: 1973 report (brief); passage explicitly says predictions made in 1972
partA.predictor: unnamed correspondents as reported by James Lighthill
partA.problems: Not Lighthill’s own prediction. Space before semicolon is typographic. The supplied lead-in is part of a longer sentence and must keep reported-speech attribution.

partA.event: machine intelligence exceeding human intelligence
partA.conditions_hedges: reported letters; when such predictions are made in 1972
partA.source_date: 1973 report (brief), reporting predictions made in 1972
partA.predictor: unnamed correspondents as reported by James Lighthill
partA.problems: Retain anonymous reported speech and possibility; not an endorsement by the report’s author.

partA.event: unknown
partA.conditions_hedges: unknown
partA.source_date: 1989 supplied by brief, not independently checked
partA.problems: HTTP 200 is an Anubis bot challenge. Original-host CDN attempt returns 403; bounded old-URL archive lookup yields no matching PDF. No passage or locator verification.

partA.event: the creation of greater than human intelligence
partA.conditions_hedges: Based largely on this trend (computer hardware progress)
partA.source_date: 1993-12 proceedings date supplied; individual article scan does not print that date
partA.problems: Includes computer networks, interfaces and biological enhancement as possible paths; do not narrow all routes to disembodied AI. The adjacent absolute-date clarification belongs to the same forecast.

partA.event: the creation of greater than human intelligence
partA.horizon: before 2005 or after 2030 (surprise outside these bounds)
partA.conditions_hedges: explicit clarification of relative-time ambiguity
partA.source_date: 1993-12 proceedings date supplied; not printed on individual scanned article
partA.problems: The source itself prints “let me more specific”. The interval is expressed by surprise, not a numeric probability or a categorical deadline.

partA.event: Singularity
partA.confidence: seems like a reasonable upper bound
partA.conditions_hedges: given the current rate of progress
partA.problems: Archive capture actually retrieved. Bounds are qualified rhetoric, not a calibrated distribution. Desired 2005–2008 completion elsewhere is distinct from this upper-bound statement.

partA.event: superhuman artificial intelligence
partA.horizon: within the first third of the next century
partA.conditions_hedges: argument rather than certainty
partA.source_date: Originally published 1998; page also says (1997), revised 25 October 1998; postscripts 2000/2005/2008
partA.problems: Redirected live copy contains later postscripts. No contemporary archive authentication; distinguish the base paper from revisions. Do not convert the horizon to a precise year.

partA.event: the required computational power will be reached
partA.conditions_hedges: If we need 100 Tops to simulate the human brain; doubling time of 12 or 18 months; best experimental supercomputers, not necessarily access for AI researchers
partA.source_date: 1998 base paper; live revision/postscript history through 2008
partA.problems: Hardware threshold, not completed superhuman AI. Following sentence allows up to an additional decade for researcher access.

partA.event: the required hardware will be available in cheap machines
partA.conditions_hedges: Based on extrapolation of past trends and on examination of technologies under development
partA.source_date: Volume 1 1998; Received Dec.1997; Fourth Draft Not Quite Final Version
partA.problems: Hardware availability rather than implemented human-level software; preserve version notice and analogy/extrapolation.

partA.event: robot intelligence will surpass our own
partA.conditions_hedges: The path I’ve outlined roughly recapitulates the evolution of human intelligence—but 10 million times more rapidly
partA.source_date: 1999 Scientific American copy; December supplied by brief
partA.problems: Forecast grounded in outlined development path, rather than an unqualified calendar certainty; live author-hosted scan transcription.

partA.event: supercomputers will achieve one human brain capacity; personal computers will do so
partA.conditions_hedges: In line with my earlier predictions; estimated computational brain capacity
partA.source_date: March 7, 2001; page date
partA.problems: Computational capacity and hardware classes must be retained; not an autonomous general-intelligence forecast. Keep distinct from the $1,000 model result in item 18.

partA.event: one Human Brain capability (2 * 10^16 cps) for $1,000
partA.conditions_hedges: from this analysis; model assumptions on knowledge, computing and feedback
partA.source_date: March 7, 2001; page date
partA.problems: Cost and computational metric are essential. Same article also prints around 2020 for personal computers; do not reconcile by deleting one expression or treating it as an edit.

partA.event: development of human-level machine intelligence
partA.conditions_hedges: Assuming no global catastrophe halts progress; explanatory question also conditions on no wars, no disasters and beneficial political/economic development
partA.source_date: 2011-06-17; post date (embedded postedAt agrees)
partA.problems: Map the three dates in question order; interviewer supplies condition and framing. Not an unconditional distribution.

partA.event: human-level AI to be reached
partA.conditions_hedges: various experts strongly disagree; assessment at AGI-09
partA.source_date: 2011 publication; this file version:20 April 2011; research conducted at AGI-09
partA.predictor: Baum, Goertzel and Goertzel survey report
partA.problems: Report-level qualitative synthesis, not respondents as a collective predictor or authors’ own numeric forecast. Preserve disagreement and selected conference population.

partA.event: high-level machine intelligence will be developed
partA.probability: one in two chance; nine in ten chance
partA.conditions_hedges: assume that human scientific activity continues without major negative disruption
partA.source_date: PDF says forthcoming 2014; questionnaire in 2012/2013
partA.problems: Abstract summary is not a pooled forecast distribution; median differs from mean. PDF p.1 and §3.2 p.9 verified with line-wrap normalisation.

partA.event: systems will move on to superintelligence
partA.horizon: in less than 30 years thereafter; within (2 years / 30 years) thereafter; within 30 years after HLMI
partA.probability: none in selected prose; table: Within 2 years median 10%, mean 19%; Within 30 years median 75%, mean 62%
partA.confidence: Experts expect; low probability; significant probability
partA.conditions_hedges: Assume for the purpose of this question that such HLMI will at some point exist
partA.source_date: PDF says forthcoming 2014; survey 2012/2013
partA.problems: Abstract less-than 30 phrasing and question within 30 differ slightly. Keep conditional anchor and table aggregation; do not turn a distribution into a fixed arrival deadline.

partA.event: AI outperforming humans in all tasks
partA.conditions_hedges: survey definition: unaided machines can accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers
partA.source_date: 24 May 2017 arXiv v 1; survey 2016 (figure axis Years from 2016)
partA.problems: Aggregate mixture forecast, not median respondent or prediction by every respondent; keep relative horizon.

partA.event: automating all human jobs
partA.conditions_hedges: distinct employment-framed question from all-task HLMI
partA.source_date: 24 May 2017 arXiv v 1; survey 2016
partA.problems: Full job automation framing differs from all tasks, despite logical similarity. Not a forecast of adoption or realised unemployment.

partA.event: AI will outperform humans in many activities; translating languages; writing high-school essays; driving a truck
partA.horizon: in the next ten years; by 2024; by 2026; by 2027
partA.probability: none in abstract excerpt; task results use 50% thresholds in report
partA.conditions_hedges: task-specific survey definitions and aggregate forecasts
partA.source_date: 24 May 2017 arXiv v 1; survey 2016
partA.problems: Three tasks with distinct dates; records should preserve task details rather than collapse to generic AGI. Line-end outper-form normalised.

partA.event: human-level machine intelligence being achieved
partA.conditions_hedges: in aggregate; cross-sectional late 2019 survey; scientific activity continues without major negative disruption
partA.source_date: 8 Jun 2022 arXiv v 1; survey fielded late 2019
partA.problems: Do not date elicitation to 2022. Abstract differentiates recontacted panel, whose aggregate shifted to 2076, from main 2060 result.

partA.event: HLMI
partA.conditions_hedges: conditional on “human scientific activity continu[ing] without major negative disruption.”; HLMI questions only; not Full Automation of Labor
partA.source_date: live survey results page; August 2022 supplied by brief; no contemporary capture checked yet
partA.problems: Equal mixture of fitted gamma distributions; 37 is rounded 36.6, not median respondent. The quotation’s nested punctuation differs typographically. Historical publication wording remains unauthenticated until capture.

partA.event: unaided machines outperforming humans in every possible task
partA.conditions_hedges: If science continues undisrupted
partA.source_date: 5 Jan 2024 arXiv v 1; report on 2023 survey
partA.predictor: Grace and colleagues Thousands of AI Authors survey report
partA.problems: Aggregate forecast; preserve conditional and universal task scope; not author personal belief or every respondent’s estimate.

partA.event: all human occupations becoming fully automatable
partA.conditions_hedges: question retains undisrupted science; fully automatable rather than actual adoption
partA.source_date: 5 Jan 2024 arXiv v 1; report on 2023 survey
partA.predictor: Grace and colleagues Thousands of AI Authors survey report
partA.problems: Separate employment framing from item 28. Keep as late as and do not interpret feasibility as jobs actually disappearing.

partA.event: no computer - or “machine intelligence” - will have passed the Turing Test
partA.conditions_hedges: bet-specific detailed test conditions
partA.source_date: 2002–2029 bet duration on live header; no exact bet-made day verified
partA.predictor: Mitchell Kapor, predictor; Ray Kurzweil, challenger
partA.problems: Negative proposition belongs to Kapor; Kurzweil takes opposing side. $20,000 stakes and named beneficiary charities match. Live header alone does not authenticate 2002 version or detailed terms.

partA.event: Emergence of the generally agreed upon “next big thing” in AI beyond deep learning
partA.confidence: I believe it will happen (date conventions)
partA.conditions_hedges: NET means “No Earlier Than”; BY means “By”; generally agreed upon
partA.source_date: January 1,2018; post heading
partA.problems: Both bounds required, not arrival in 2023 or deadline-only 2027. Date-convention typography differs; intervening formatting is not a substantive omission. Live page has later comments and navigation.

partA.event: An AI system with an ongoing existence (no day is the repeat of another day as it currently is for all AI systems) at the level of a mouse
partA.conditions_hedges: No Earlier Than; ongoing existence requirement
partA.source_date: January 1,2018; post heading
partA.problems: Lower bound only, not “by 2030”. Mouse-level without ongoing-existence condition loses the proposition.

partA.event: A robot that seems as intelligent, as attentive, and as faithful, as a dog
partA.conditions_hedges: No Earlier Than; intelligence, attention and faithfulness together
partA.source_date: January 1,2018; post heading
partA.problems: Lower bound, not a deadline; seems is part of the event criterion.

partA.event: transformative AI
partA.horizon: within 15 years (by 2036); within 40 years (by 2060); this century (by 2100)
partA.probability: more than a 10% chance; a~50% chance; a~2/3 chance
partA.conditions_hedges: AI powerful enough to bring us into a new, qualitatively different future
partA.source_date: Sep 7,2021; page publication date
partA.problems: Keep both relative and absolute expressions as printed, even though 40 years/by 2060 are not arithmetically identical from 2021. Do not silently “correct” source.

partA.event: an existential catastrophe of this kind
partA.conditions_hedges: of this kind: power-seeking misaligned AI leading to full disempowerment; updated estimate differs from initial one
partA.source_date: April 2021 report; May 2022 estimate update;16 Jun 2022 arXiv v 1
partA.problems: Two estimate versions, not one 2022 forecast at 5%; do not confuse arXiv posting with original estimate.

partA.event: transformative AI
partA.confidence: roughly; at the time; bottom line estimates
partA.conditions_hedges: retrospective account of modelling done~May 2019 to~Jul 2020 and posted Sep 2020
partA.source_date: 2 Aug 2022; retrospective post about 2020 estimates
partA.predictor: Ajeya Cotra retrospectively describing her earlier modelling estimates
partA.problems: Both fragments occur, separated by parentheticals and bullets; ellipsis is editorial, so not a single word-for-word passage. The 2022 post is not the original 2020 estimate document.

partA.event: transformative AI
partA.horizon: by 2030; by 2036; A median of~2040; by 2050
partA.confidence: I now expect something roughly like this; pretty volatile
partA.conditions_hedges: updated estimates; contrasts with prior~2050 median
partA.source_date: 2 Aug 2022; update post
partA.problems: Current median~2040, not~2050. Opening 2050 belongs to retrospective baseline. Preserve approximations and expected volatility.

partA.event: AGI
partA.conditions_hedges: trend extrapolation in compute, algorithmic efficiencies and unhobbling
partA.source_date: June 2024 supplied; chapter opening has no day date
partA.problems: Plausibility, not certainty or a numeric probability. Do not map AGI to a different event definition without source context.

partA.event: generalist AI systems will outperform human abilities across many critical domains
partA.horizon: within this decade or the next
partA.conditions_hedges: Combined with ongoing growth and automation in AI R&D
partA.source_date: 26 Oct 2023 arXiv v 1
partA.problems: Possibility and many critical domains, not necessarily every task or unconditional expectation. Line-wrap hyphenation normalised.

partA.event: AI systems will exceed expert skill level in most domains, and carry out as much productive activity as one of today’s largest corporations
partA.conditions_hedges: Given the picture as we see it now
partA.source_date: May 22,2023; publication; archive capture 20230522175341
partA.predictor: Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, Ilya Sutskever
partA.problems: Live 403 resolved by contemporary original blog capture. Quoted fragment occurs in opening paragraph; full sentence also has productive-activity criterion. Possibility is not a commitment or numeric likelihood.

partA.event: superintelligence
partA.conditions_hedges: While superintelligence seems far off now
partA.source_date: July 5,2023; publication; archive capture 20230705170451
partA.problems: Live 403 resolved by contemporary original blog capture. Footnote marker is not a wording change; distinguish possible arrival from separate four-year alignment research goal.

partA.event: superintelligence
partA.confidence: It is possible; I’m confident we’ll get there
partA.conditions_hedges: it may take longer
partA.source_date: September 23,2024; page date
partA.problems: Confidence in eventual arrival is not confidence in the few-thousand-days horizon.

partA.event: powerful AI will be built
partA.conditions_hedges: though there are also ways it could take much longer
partA.source_date: October 2024; essay date
partA.problems: Powerful AI is defined in following list; essay’s 5–10-year effects clock begins after arrival. Preserve lower possibility and long-tail hedge.

partA.event: the first AI agents “join the workforce” and materially change the output of companies
partA.conditions_hedges: both workforce participation and material output effect
partA.source_date: 2025-01-05 supplied by brief; page body has no printed day and inspected body metadata did not expose it
partA.problems: Personal blog attribution, not automatically formal institutional guarantee. Neighboring AGI confidence statement is not the same event.

partA.event: marshall the intellectual capacity equivalent to everyone in 2025; everyone should have access to unlimited genius to direct however they can imagine
partA.confidence: should be able to; should have access
partA.conditions_hedges: preceding discussion: distribution, early intervention and access policy
partA.source_date: 2025-02-09 supplied by brief; day not independently printed in inspected body
partA.problems: Normative and capability/access language coexist; do not turn should into a guaranteed rollout or treat 2025 as the horizon. Source spelling marshall retained.

partA.event: powerful AI systems will emerge
partA.conditions_hedges: As our CEO Dario Amodei writes in “Machines of Loving Grace”
partA.source_date: Mar 6,2025; Published date
partA.problems: Institutional expectation; not identical to original essay’s as-early-as 2026 hedge. Preserve the attribution without overwriting the earlier version. Link-boundary whitespace normalised.

partA.event: the impact of superhuman AI over the next decade will be enormous, exceeding that of the Industrial Revolution
partA.conditions_hedges: scenario represents our best guess about what that might look like
partA.source_date: April 3 rd 2025; page date
partA.predictor: Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, Thomas Larsen, Eli Lifland, Romeo Dean
partA.problems: Scenario framing and impact prediction are distinct; opening sentence alone is not a calibrated claim that a specific model will exist in 2027. Live page has later navigation links.

partA.event: powerful AI systems are developed
partA.confidence: highly uncertain; we find it plausible
partA.conditions_hedges: assumption 2 Timelines; motivates an anytime safety approach
partA.source_date: 2 Apr 2025; arXiv v 1
partA.predictor: Rohin Shah and coauthors (paper, primarily Google DeepMind)
partA.problems: Plausible planning assumption, not an institutional certainty or a numerical probability. Preserve uncertainty.

partA.event: AI systems equivalent to a “country of geniuses in a datacenter”
partA.conditions_hedges: As I’ve written elsewhere
partA.source_date: April 2025; essay date
partA.problems: Keep capability metaphor and possibility. This timing is separate from interpretability’s 5–10-year development estimate. Link whitespace normalised.

partA.event: systems that can figure out novel insights
partA.conditions_hedges: none
partA.source_date: 2025-06-10 supplied by brief; not independently printed in inspected body
partA.problems: Likely, not definite; narrower event than general AGI.

partA.event: robots that can do tasks in the real world
partA.conditions_hedges: none
partA.source_date: 2025-06-10 supplied by brief; not independently printed in inspected body
partA.problems: Possibility, not a firm deadline; do not add a level of task generality not stated here.

partA.event: powerful AI
partA.conditions_hedges: although it could also be considerably further out; As I wrote in Machines of Loving Grace
partA.source_date: January 2026; essay date
partA.problems: Relative horizon, not a converted year range; historical reference to another essay does not establish the original wording there. Link whitespace normalised.

partA.event: AI is better than humans at essentially everything
partA.horizon: more than a few years (cannot possibly be)
partA.conditions_hedges: If the exponential continues—which is not certain, but now has a decade-long track record supporting it
partA.source_date: January 2026; essay date
partA.problems: Conditional upper-bound rhetoric, not an unconditional few-year certainty. Keep uncertainty of trend continuation.

model_review.conclusion: Do not adopt unchanged. The document-to-literal approach fits the documentary layer, but several checked records do not fit the proposed validation/form rules cleanly.

cases.issue: The event is a labelled contextual paraphrase; the quoted bound sentence does not itself contain Singularity. The proposal allows labelled paraphrase in its field table but then requires every event inside an evidence quotation. Preserve an explicit paraphrase/context route.
Should be able to combines future capability and an aim. It is not a clean unqualified forecast. Require an ambiguous forecast/aim mode, or an explicit scope decision; preserve should.

Versioned estimates and multi-point forecasts need structured associations between event, horizon, probability and estimate version. A single free-text probability block does not safely encode two Carlsmith versions, all four Cotra points, or both Kurzweil hardware classes.

Authorship alone cannot recover predictor identity or position. Lighthill reports unnamed correspondents; the bet has opposing parties. Keep reporter, reported speaker and bet position explicit; allow unknown identities without inventing person entities.

Publication, speech/poll/estimate date, reprint/version and capture attestation must be separate. Within ten years in a1957 address is not automatically anchored to1958 print publication. interval.from must retain the source-supplied anchor.

model_review.validation: Do not prohibit contested/unresolved documentary-attribution or version disputes categorically. This does not authorize outcome assessment. Supported can mean only that the source states the scoped prediction; held/unretrieved wording must not become supported by schema default. Period, relative and figure horizons stay unconverted.
